title: Leveraging Process-Action Epistemic Network Analysis to Illuminate Student Self-Regulated Learning with a Socratic Chatbot
extended_summary:
This study examines how student interactions with a generative AI Socratic chatbot can be analyzed through a self-regulated learning (SRL) lens. The authors aimed to answer two questions: how chatbot conversations can be processed using an SRL framework, and how interaction patterns differ across student ability and learning-gain groups. The work is positioned as a learning analytics study focused on understanding, rather than definitively proving, how chatbot-supported learning relates to SRL behaviors.

The intervention was an in-house Socratic chatbot for an introductory undergraduate statistics course. Unlike answer-giving chatbots, it was prompt-engineered to respond with scaffolded questions that encourage students to reason through concepts independently. Students completed a pre-test, participated in a three-week pilot course using asynchronous blended learning with required chatbot interaction and online videos, and then completed a post-test. Chat logs were coded using a process-action SRL framework and analyzed with epistemic network analysis and ordered network analysis.

The study involved 34 undergraduate students in a three-week pilot class at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. The first week was onsite and the following two weeks were online, all conducted asynchronously, with no human tutor involved. Students interacted with the chatbot at their own pace while learning introductory statistics content.

The authors report significant pre-post score improvement overall, but the main findings concern behavioral differences in chatbot use. Higher-ability students showed more goal-setting, review, organization, and reflective/evaluative behaviors, whereas lower-ability students focused more on information searching. Students with higher learning gains were more likely to ask fundamental conceptual questions and seek examples, while medium-gain students were more likely to paste in problem statements and focus on complex problem solving. The paper concludes that learning analytics from chatbot interactions can reveal meaningful SRL patterns and can inform more adaptive chatbot prompting and scaffolding, though results should be interpreted cautiously given the pilot design and limited sample.

identified_tools.name: Socratic chatbot
identified_tools.description: An educational chatbot designed to support learning through Socratic dialogue and guided questioning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an introductory undergraduate statistics pilot class during a 3-week asynchronous blended course. Thirty-four undergraduates interacted with the chatbot at their own pace alongside online videos, without a human tutor. The study used pre-course and post-course assessments and analyzed chatbot interaction patterns across ability and learning-gain groups.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 34 undergraduates, post-course statistics test scores were significantly higher than pre-course scores following the 3-week course that included chatbot use. The mean gain was approximately 27.21 points (SD=21.18), with p<0.001 and a large within-sample effect size of about d≈1.28.
findings.measure: pre-course versus post-course statistics test score

findings.finding_summary: Interaction analyses indicated that higher-scoring students more often engaged in reflective and evaluative self-regulated learning activities, whereas lower-scoring students more often focused on searching for answers. No effect size was reported for these group differences.
findings.measure: SRL interaction patterns in chatbot conversations, including reflective/evaluative activities versus answer-searching behaviors

findings.finding_summary: Ordered epistemic network analysis suggested that learning-gain groups differed in their chatbot interaction patterns, with higher gains associated with more concept-questioning and example-seeking behaviors. No numeric effect size was reported.
findings.measure: association between chatbot interaction behaviors and learning gains, especially concept-questioning and example-seeking behaviors

quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pre-post study with an educational intervention and quantitative analyses, but it lacks a control group, uses a small pilot sample, and was conducted at a single site over a short duration.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically significant pre-post improvement with a large within-sample effect (d ≈ 1.28), but because there is no control group, the causal impact of the chatbot intervention is unclear; impact evidence is therefore suggestive rather than definitive.
